aspect: Hardware envelope & local constraints for building/training a small diffusion LLM on a consumer laptop — Economics / how

findings.claim: Canonical training-memory formula: mixed-precision AdamW training needs ~16 bytes/parameter before activations — 2 B/param fp16/bf16 weights + 4 B/param gradients (fp32) or 2 B (fp16) + 12 B/param AdamW optimizer states (fp32 master copy 4 + momentum 4 + variance 4). 8-bit optimizers cut optimizer states to 6 B/param; SGD+momentum is 8 B/param. Inference is ~1.2x model weights. So a 124M-param model trains in roughly 2-2.5 GB + activations — comfortably inside an 8 GB laptop GPU.
findings.title: Transformer Math 101 — EleutherAI blog

findings.claim: Compute budgeting formula: total training FLOPs C ≈ 6PD (2PD forward + 4PD backward), and activation memory with full recomputation collapses to 2·s·b·h·L bytes (vs sbhL(10+24/t+5as/ht) without recomputation). This lets you size a laptop run: params x tokens fixes the FLOPs bill regardless of hardware.
findings.title: Transformer Math 101 — EleutherAI blog

findings.claim: Best recent single-consumer-GPU pretraining anchor: a 163M-param GPT-2-small-class model was trained from scratch on one RTX 3090 (24 GB) in ~44-48 h on 3.2B FineWeb tokens at ~19,921 tokens/s using AMP + TF32 (22% speedup over fp32), reaching val loss 3.69-3.94; weights ~670 MB, optimizer state ~1.3 GB in checkpoints; total ~3.2e18 FLOPs. Extrapolating a laptop 4060/4070 as roughly 2-4x slower (memory-bandwidth- and TGP-bound) puts the same run at ~4-8 days; that extrapolation is my inference, the measured numbers are direct.
findings.title: Writing an LLM from scratch, part 28 — training a base model from scratch on an RTX 3090 (Giles Thomas)

findings.claim: nanoGPT's hardware ladder defines the consumer envelope: shakespeare-char toy (6-layer, 384-dim) trains in ~3 min on an A100; a shrunk config (4 layers, 4 heads, 128 embd, block 64, batch 12) trains on CPU-only in ~3 min to loss 1.88 with --device=cpu --compile=False; Apple Silicon --device=mps gives '2-3X' over CPU; full GPT-2 124M reproduction needs 'at least an 8X A100 40GB node' for ~4 days; Windows users must pass --compile=False.
findings.title: karpathy/nanoGPT README

findings.claim: Naive worst-case single-GPU anchor: a user training nanoGPT GPT-2 124M on one RTX 4090 (PyTorch 2.0 nightly, batch 12, grad-accum 5, block 1024) measured ~5 s/iteration, i.e. ~35 days for the full 600k-iteration run, while noting the config seemed suboptimal. Modern tuned runs (see Giles Thomas finding) are ~15-20x faster per token, so treat 35 days as an untuned floor, not an expectation.
findings.title: Training Time for 1x 4090 GPU — nanoGPT issue #179

findings.claim: On a Windows laptop with an 8 GB RTX 4060, the usable AI VRAM budget is realistically ~6.5-7.2 GB, not 8 GB, because Windows 11, browsers, and drivers hold GPU memory; and 'a smaller model fully on GPU is usually better than a larger model half offloaded'. Mobile 4060s are additionally limited by laptop power, cooling, memory bandwidth, and vendor tuning, so sustained performance varies between machines.
findings.title: Laptop RTX 4060 8GB Local AI Guide (knightli.com)

findings.claim: Laptop GPU wattage (TGP) dominates real performance: the RTX 4070 Laptop is configurable 35-115 W (+15-25 W Dynamic Boost), boost clock 1230-2175 MHz depending on TGP, and a 140 W variant is only ~36% faster than a 65 W variant in 3DMark Time Spy (105 W vs 120 W differ ~1%). Two laptops with the same GPU name can differ 30-50% in throughput — training-time estimates must be per-machine, not per-GPU-name.
findings.title: Comparing all RTX 4070s: 65W/105W/120W/140W TGP — LaptopMedia (specs corroborated by Notebookcheck)

findings.claim: Windows-specific VRAM-overflow trap: since driver 536.40 NVIDIA enables 'CUDA Sysmem Fallback', which spills GPU allocations into system RAM instead of OOM-ing. Training that exceeds VRAM silently slows to a crawl (VRAM ~hundreds of GB/s vs PCIe gen4 x16 ~25 GB/s per direction); the fix is NVIDIA Control Panel -> 'CUDA - Sysmem Fallback Policy' -> 'Prefer No Sysmem Fallback' so jobs fail fast instead of running 10-50x slow.
findings.title: NVIDIA support: System Memory Fallback for Stable Diffusion (plus PyTorch forums 'Documented fix: Slow execution, Pytorch using GPU shared memory')

findings.claim: Precision choice on consumer hardware: bf16 has fp32's dynamic range and needs no loss scaling — the 2025/2026 default on Ampere+ (all RTX 30/40 laptop GPUs) — while fp16 requires GradScaler-style loss scaling to avoid underflow (values <~6e-5) / overflow (>65504) and is mainly needed on pre-Ampere cards. Nuance: fp16 carries more mantissa precision than bf16, which one 2025 paper exploits to fix training-inference mismatch; for a small math-focused model either works, but bf16 is the low-friction default.
findings.title: Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16 (arXiv 2510.26788) + zeroentropy.dev mixed-precision concepts

findings.claim: Gradient/activation checkpointing trades ~one extra forward pass for large activation-memory savings: measured slowdowns across sources span ~22-33% for 50-80% activation-memory reduction (the exact percentage is workload-dependent and no single official number exists). PyTorch's Memory Budget API for torch.compile (experimental in 2.4) shows '50% memory reduction by recomputing only pointwise ops', and Selective Activation Checkpointing landed as prototype in 2.5. On an 8 GB laptop GPU this is the main lever to afford longer sequences/bigger batches.
findings.title: Current and New Activation Checkpointing Techniques in PyTorch (pytorch.org blog)

findings.claim: 8-bit Adam (bitsandbytes) cuts optimizer-state memory 75% (8 B/param -> 2 B/param) 'without losing any accuracy' and with no hyperparameter retuning; it helps parameter-heavy memory budgets but not activation-dominated ones. Integrated in HF Trainer via optim='paged_adamw_8bit'. Caveat for this project: bitsandbytes is Linux/CUDA-first and Windows support has historically lagged (medium confidence on that caveat).
findings.title: 8-bit optimizers — bitsandbytes documentation (Hugging Face)

findings.claim: CPU-only training is viable only at toy scale: nanoGPT's CPU path trains a ~1M-param char-level model in minutes, but a GSM8K-capable model (tens of millions of params, billions of tokens) is off the table — a single A100 needs ~10 h for even a 1-layer LM on real data, and CPUs are 1-2 orders of magnitude slower than that. Practical CPU-only ceiling for this project: <10M params, char/digit-level arithmetic tasks, hours-to-days timescale.
findings.title: karpathy/nanoGPT README (CPU config) + corroborating training-time data points

findings.claim: The 'Cramming' study (Geiping & Goldstein) showed a BERT-class masked language model can be trained from scratch to near-BERT performance on a single consumer GPU in 24 hours, and that 'performance closely follows scaling laws observed in large-compute settings' even at this scale — evidence that one-GPU-day budgets produce genuinely useful masked-objective models (directly relevant since masked diffusion LM training is a masked-prediction objective).
findings.title: Cramming: Training a Language Model on a Single GPU in One Day (arXiv 2212.14034)

findings.claim: The diffusion tax, quantified: masked diffusion models (MDMs) follow scaling laws with rates comparable to autoregressive models but need ~16x more pre-training compute to match ARM likelihood/generation performance ('MDMs with 16 times more pre-training time offer a flexible trade-off against ARMs'). Encouraging for this project: their 1.1B MDM was competitive with 7B Llama-2 on GSM8K math reasoning — masked diffusion punches above its weight on math benchmarks specifically.
findings.title: Scaling up Masked Diffusion Models on Text (Nie et al., arXiv 2410.18514)

findings.claim: The diffusion tax reverses in exactly the laptop regime: in data-constrained settings with repeated epochs over limited data, masked diffusion 'significantly outperform[s] AR models when compute is abundant but data is scarce', because randomized masking acts as implicit data augmentation over token orderings; the paper derives new scaling laws and 'a closed-form expression for the critical compute threshold' where diffusion becomes preferable. A small fixed math corpus (GSM8K + synthetic arithmetic) trained for many epochs is precisely this regime.
findings.title: Diffusion Beats Autoregressive in Data-Constrained Settings (Prabhudesai et al., CMU/Lambda, arXiv 2507.15857)

findings.claim: Windows toolchain friction #1: torch.compile is unsupported on native Windows because official Triton wheels don't exist for Windows; options are (a) run with compile disabled (slower but works), (b) the community triton-windows fork (bundles TinyCC since 3.2.0.post13; PyTorch now points at it as fallback), or (c) WSL2. Plan for a 1.2-2x throughput loss if you skip compilation.
findings.title: woct0rdho/triton-windows + pytorch/pytorch issue #122094 'Investigate torch.compile Windows support'

findings.claim: Windows toolchain friction #2: pip install flash-attn routinely fails to build on Windows (hours-long compiles, C++ toolchain and CUDA/PyTorch version mismatch errors; Windows support only 'might work' since v2.3.2). The reliable consumer-hardware path is PyTorch's built-in F.scaled_dot_product_attention (SDPA), which needs no compilation and has fused kernels on RTX 30/40; community-prebuilt Windows wheels exist as a secondary option.
findings.title: How to get Flash-Attention under Windows 11 CUDA — Dao-AILab/flash-attention issue #1469 (plus issue #1421)

findings.claim: WSL2 is the lower-friction Windows path for CUDA training (full Linux toolchain: triton, bitsandbytes, flash-attn), with one architecture rule — the NVIDIA driver lives on Windows; never install a driver inside WSL2 (apt driver installs are the #1 breakage). Known tradeoff: WSL2 CUDA does not respect the 'Sysmem Fallback Policy', so over-VRAM allocations hard-OOM in WSL2 rather than spilling — arguably better for training (fail fast) but a behavioral difference to know.
findings.title: WSL2 CUDA Does Not Respect 'CUDA - Sysmem Fallback Policy' — microsoft/WSL issue #11050 (plus WSL2 CUDA setup guides)

findings.claim: Apple Silicon (MPS) works for small-model training (~2-3x over CPU per nanoGPT) with unified memory removing the discrete-VRAM ceiling, but carries hazards: unsupported ops need PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1; AMP/mixed-precision support is limited with no tensor-core-style speedup; memory pressure causes SSD-swap collapse; and MPS had a silent-corruption class of bug — addcmul_/addcdiv_ silently not writing to non-contiguous tensors, which froze Adam updates entirely (fixed in PyTorch >=2.4; macOS 15+ adds native non-contiguous Metal support). Minimum safe stack: PyTorch >=2.4 + macOS 15.
findings.title: The bug that taught me more about PyTorch than years of using it — Elana Simon (plus Lightning MPS docs, tillcode.com MPS guide)

findings.claim: Economics of local vs rented: cloud RTX 4090s rent for ~$0.29-0.69/hr typical (market range $0.17-1.61/hr across 14+ providers; Vast.ai spot from ~$0.29, RunPod secure ~$0.34-0.69). A 48-hour GPT-2-small-class pretraining run therefore costs ~$15-35 rented — versus roughly $1-2 of electricity but 2-5x the wall-clock (4-10 days) on a 60-115 W laptop GPU (prices are direct from the aggregator; the laptop wall-clock multiple and electricity figure are my arithmetic from TGP specs). Rational split: prototype + UI + final finetune locally; rent one 4090-day (~$10) only if from-scratch pretraining stalls.
findings.title: RTX 4090 Cloud Pricing: Compare 14+ Providers (getdeploying.com)

failed: No rigorous published transformer-TRAINING throughput benchmark specifically for laptop RTX 4060/4070 (search surfaced inference-only benchmarks and SEO listicles; closest usable anchors are desktop 3090/4090 practitioner numbers)
Reddit-style firsthand 'trained GPT-2 overnight on laptop 4060' anecdotes — search returned mostly repos and blogs, not direct laptop wall-clock reports
CPU-only training query returned mostly irrelevant arXiv papers; had to reconstruct the CPU ceiling from nanoGPT's own CPU config
HF perf_train_gpu_one docs fetch returned only a version-redirect page (claims sourced elsewhere instead)

contradictions: Diffusion compute penalty: Nie et al. (2410.18514) quantify ~16x more pretraining compute for MDM-vs-AR parity, but Prabhudesai et al. (2507.15857) show diffusion BEATS AR under data-constrained multi-epoch training, and a 2025 GIDD scaling study (alphaXiv summary of 2512.10858) argues the 'up to 16x' estimates were methodologically limited and that a simple cross-entropy objective makes MDMs ~12% more FLOPs-efficient. Resolution for this project: the 16x tax applies to single-epoch web-scale likelihood parity; a small fixed math corpus trained many epochs is the regime where the tax shrinks or reverses.

Single-GPU GPT-2 training time: nanoGPT issue #179 implies ~35 days on a 4090 (5 s/iter, early PyTorch 2.0 nightly, self-described suboptimal), while Giles Thomas (Dec 2025) trained a comparable 163M model on a slower RTX 3090 in ~44-48 h at ~20k tok/s. The 15-20x gap is tuning + AMP/TF32 + modern PyTorch, not hardware — old anecdotes systematically overstate consumer training times.

Gradient checkpointing cost: sources disagree on the slowdown — ~22% (one measured case), ~30% ('throughput tax'), ~33% (one extra forward) — and the official PyTorch blog declines to give a single number; treat it as 20-35% workload-dependent.

8 GB VRAM adequacy: desktop RTX 4060 benchmarking (marketcalls.in, Jan 2025) concludes 8 GB is 'plenty' for small-model work (~5 GB peak in their tests), while the laptop-focused guide (knightli) says only 6.5-7.2 GB is actually usable on Windows laptops — both true; the delta is Windows compositor/browser overhead plus laptop vendor tuning.

WSL2 vs native Windows: WSL2 gives the full Linux ML toolchain (triton, flash-attn, bitsandbytes) and is broadly recommended, yet WSL2 ignores the NVIDIA sysmem-fallback setting (microsoft/WSL #11050), so behavior at the VRAM ceiling differs: native Windows silently slows (spill), WSL2 hard-OOMs. Neither is strictly better; the plan must handle both.

FP16 vs BF16: consensus says bf16 is the stability default on Ampere+, but arXiv 2510.26788 argues fp16's extra mantissa precision fixes training-inference mismatch in RL fine-tuning — a reminder that 'bf16 always' is a default, not a law.
practitionerReality: What practitioners actually hit, in order: (1) The VRAM ceiling arrives before the compute ceiling — a 124-163M-param model in bf16+AdamW is only ~2-2.6 GB of states, so on 8 GB the real budget fight is activations, solved with micro-batch 2-12 + gradient accumulation + activation checkpointing rather than exotic tricks (a ~355M model fits a 16 GB 4060-class card at seq 1024, batch 2, accum 16, bf16 per the bitrifttech chatbot-tutorial repo). (2) Laptop numbers are per-machine, not per-GPU: TGP (35-140 W) and cooling cause 30-50% throughput spread between two laptops with identical GPU names, and sustained training throttles further; desktop-GPU benchmarks overestimate laptops by roughly 2x. (3) Windows is the pitfall zone: silent sysmem spill makes runs mysteriously 10-50x slower (set 'Prefer No Sysmem Fallback'), torch.compile needs triton-windows or must be disabled, flash-attn rarely builds — practitioners either accept plain SDPA without compile or move to WSL2. (4) On Macs, MPS is fine for the small models this project needs but has a history of silent numerical bugs (frozen Adam updates on non-contiguous tensors, fixed in torch 2.4) — pin PyTorch >=2.4, watch for parameters that stop moving, and expect swap-collapse if model + OS exceed unified memory. (5) Economically, nobody should suffer a marginal local run: a rented 4090 at ~$0.35/hr does a laptop-week of training for ~$10-30, so the rational local envelope is prototyping, the visualization UI, small (5-60M param) diffusion models trained hours-to-overnight, and GSM8K-style finetunes — with cloud as a pressure valve, not a requirement.
gaps: No published transformer-TRAINING (not inference) tokens/sec benchmark specifically for laptop RTX 4060/4070 GPUs — the plan must extrapolate from desktop 3090/4090 anchors with a 2-4x derating, and should include an early empirical throughput probe on the actual machine.

No verified wall-clock report of anyone training a small DIFFUSION language model on a laptop — MDLM/SEDD/LLaDA-class repos assume A100+ clusters; the 16x-compute and data-constrained findings let us reason about it, but the exact laptop cost of a masked-diffusion objective vs AR at 10-100M params is unverified territory.
Cramming paper abstract does not name the exact GPU used; I did not verify the GPU model from the paper body, so it is cited only for the one-GPU-one-day feasibility and scaling-law claims.

Prabhudesai et al.'s exact numeric epoch thresholds (e.g., how many epochs of data reuse before diffusion overtakes AR, the decay constant) were not visible on the abstract page — the closed-form critical-compute expression exists but its constants need extraction from the PDF during planning.
Publication date of EleutherAI's Transformer Math 101 (April 2023) and of the LaptopMedia TGP comparison were not independently confirmed on-page.
MPS bf16/AMP current status (2026) not verified against official PyTorch release notes — only secondary guides saying support is 'limited/evolving'.
Electricity-cost claim (~$1-2 for a multi-day laptop run) is arithmetic from TGP specs, not a sourced measurement.

bestSources.title: Transformer Math 101 — EleutherAI
bestSources.why: The single load-bearing source for the whole hardware envelope: exact bytes-per-parameter for weights/gradients/optimizer states under every precision regime, activation-memory formulas with/without recomputation, and C≈6PD compute budgeting — everything needed to size a model to 6-8 GB of laptop VRAM on paper before writing code.

bestSources.title: Scaling up Masked Diffusion Models on Text (arXiv 2410.18514)
bestSources.why: Quantifies the economics of choosing diffusion: ~16x pretraining-compute tax vs AR for parity, MDM scaling laws, and — critically for this project — evidence that a 1.1B MDM matches 7B Llama-2 on GSM8K, showing math reasoning is a relative strength of masked diffusion.

bestSources.title: Diffusion Beats Autoregressive in Data-Constrained Settings (arXiv 2507.15857)
bestSources.why: Flips the 16x tax in the laptop's favor: with limited data and many epochs (exactly a local math-corpus build), randomized masking acts as implicit data augmentation and diffusion overtakes AR — including a closed-form critical-compute threshold to plan against.

bestSources.title: Writing an LLM from scratch, part 28 (gilesthomas.com)
bestSources.why: The most concrete, recent, end-to-end consumer-GPU pretraining datapoint found: 163M params, one RTX 3090, ~20k tok/s, 3.2B tokens in ~48 h, with memory and FLOPs accounting — the calibration anchor for scaling expectations down to laptop GPUs.

bestSources.title: karpathy/nanoGPT
bestSources.why: Canonical reference codebase whose README doubles as a hardware-ladder map: working CPU-only config (~3 min toy run), MPS guidance (2-3x), Windows --compile=False caveat, and the 8xA100 upper anchor — the de facto template the DLLM build will mirror.
